title: AP Biology — Chapter 13 (meiosis and heredity)
source: Carter's Ch 13 guide: her slide deck slides 1-51, his spoken priority list, plus the Mendel/Hardy-Weinberg half of the Fri 11/13 quiz. Refresh this file when the unit changes.

questions.stem: A karyotype from a human fetus shows 47 chromosomes, including three copies of chromosome 21 and two X chromosomes. Which description of this chromosome set is correct?
questions.correct: 45 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes, with the extra chromosome being an autosome.
distractors: 44 autosomes and 3 sex chromosomes, with the extra chromosome being a sex chromosome.
47 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes, with no sex chromosomes counted separately.
45 autosomes and 1 sex chromosome, with one X chromosome missing.
questions.why: The 47 chromosomes split into 45 autosomes plus 2 X sex chromosomes, and chromosome 21 is an autosome; the first distractor wrongly counts the extra copy as a sex chromosome.
options: 45 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes, with the extra chromosome being an autosome.
47 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes, with no sex chromosomes counted separately.
45 autosomes and 1 sex chromosome, with one X chromosome missing.
44 autosomes and 3 sex chromosomes, with the extra chromosome being a sex chromosome.

questions.stem: To make a karyotype, a technician arrests white blood cells in metaphase with a drug that prevents spindle fibers from separating chromosomes. Why does metaphase make homologs easiest to pair?
questions.correct: Chromosomes are condensed and still duplicated, so homologs can be matched by size, centromere position, and banding.
distractors: Homologs have already separated, so each chromosome can be compared with its partner independently.
Crossing over is complete, so recombinant chromosomes can be identified by their new banding patterns.
DNA is replicating, so each homolog is present as a single chromatid that can be aligned.
questions.why: At metaphase chromosomes are condensed with sister chromatids still attached, allowing homologs to be paired; the first distractor confuses metaphase with anaphase separation.
options: Homologs have already separated, so each chromosome can be compared with its partner independently.
Chromosomes are condensed and still duplicated, so homologs can be matched by size, centromere position, and banding.
DNA is replicating, so each homolog is present as a single chromatid that can be aligned.
Crossing over is complete, so recombinant chromosomes can be identified by their new banding patterns.

questions.stem: A karyotype from a healthy person shows 46 chromosomes with no visible structural abnormalities. What can be concluded from the karyotype alone?
questions.correct: No chromosome-number or large structural abnormality was detected, but a single-gene mutation could still be present.
distractors: The person cannot carry any recessive alleles because both homologs look normal.
All alleles on the person's homologous chromosomes must be identical.
Crossing over did not occur during the meiosis that produced the person's gametes.
questions.why: A karyotype detects chromosome number and large structure, not allele sequences; the second distractor wrongly equates homologous chromosomes with identical alleles.
options: The person cannot carry any recessive alleles because both homologs look normal.
Crossing over did not occur during the meiosis that produced the person's gametes.
No chromosome-number or large structural abnormality was detected, but a single-gene mutation could still be present.
All alleles on the person's homologous chromosomes must be identical.

questions.stem: A human secondary oocyte is released at ovulation and is then fertilized. What completes meiosis II, and what cells are produced?
questions.correct: Sperm entry triggers completion, producing one ovum and a second polar body.
distractors: Ovulation triggers completion, producing four ova from the secondary oocyte.
Meiosis II completes before fertilization, producing two ova from the secondary oocyte.
Fertilization blocks meiosis II, so the first polar body becomes the ovum.
questions.why: The secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase II and completes only after sperm entry, with unequal cytokinesis yielding one ovum and a polar body; the first distractor assumes four ova.
options: Meiosis II completes before fertilization, producing two ova from the secondary oocyte.
Ovulation triggers completion, producing four ova from the secondary oocyte.
Fertilization blocks meiosis II, so the first polar body becomes the ovum.
Sperm entry triggers completion, producing one ovum and a second polar body.

questions.stem: In a moss, the green leafy gametophyte is haploid and produces gametes, while the diploid sporophyte produces spores. Which statement correctly explains how these cells are made?
questions.correct: The haploid gametophyte makes gametes by mitosis, and the diploid sporophyte makes spores by meiosis.
distractors: The haploid gametophyte makes gametes by meiosis, and the diploid sporophyte makes spores by mitosis.
Both gametes and spores are made by meiosis because both are haploid cells.
Both gametes and spores are made by mitosis because both are single cells.
questions.why: Mitosis in an already haploid gametophyte preserves n, while meiosis in the diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores; the second distractor assumes any haploid product requires meiosis.
options: The haploid gametophyte makes gametes by mitosis, and the diploid sporophyte makes spores by meiosis.
The haploid gametophyte makes gametes by meiosis, and the diploid sporophyte makes spores by mitosis.
Both gametes and spores are made by meiosis because both are haploid cells.
Both gametes and spores are made by mitosis because both are single cells.

questions.stem: A human zygote with 46 chromosomes divides repeatedly to form an embryo, and later some adult gonadal cells undergo meiosis. Which pairing correctly describes the two divisions?
questions.correct: Mitosis maintains the diploid number in body cells, while meiosis halves it to produce haploid gametes.
distractors: Mitosis halves the chromosome number, while meiosis doubles it before fertilization.
Both divisions reduce the chromosome number by half in each daughter cell.
Meiosis maintains the diploid number in body cells, while mitosis produces gametes.
questions.why: Mitosis supports growth with the same diploid set, and meiosis produces haploid gametes; the third distractor swaps the roles of the two divisions.
options: Meiosis maintains the diploid number in body cells, while mitosis produces gametes.
Mitosis maintains the diploid number in body cells, while meiosis halves it to produce haploid gametes.
Both divisions reduce the chromosome number by half in each daughter cell.
Mitosis halves the chromosome number, while meiosis doubles it before fertilization.

questions.stem: At metaphase I, a human cell has 23 bivalents, or tetrads. What does each bivalent contain?
questions.correct: Two homologous chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, for four chromatids total.
distractors: Two sister chromatids from one chromosome, for two chromatids total.
Four homologous chromosomes, each with one chromatid, for four chromosomes total.
One autosome and one sex chromosome, for two chromosomes total.
questions.why: A bivalent is a paired homologous pair, and each homolog is duplicated, giving four chromatids; the first distractor confuses sister chromatids with homologs.
options: Two sister chromatids from one chromosome, for two chromatids total.
One autosome and one sex chromosome, for two chromosomes total.
Two homologous chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, for four chromatids total.
Four homologous chromosomes, each with one chromatid, for four chromosomes total.

questions.stem: A human primary spermatocyte with 46 chromosomes completes meiosis and cytokinesis normally. How many sperm are produced, and what chromosome number does each carry?
questions.correct: Four sperm, each with 23 chromosomes.
distractors: Two sperm, each with 46 chromosomes.
Four sperm, each with 46 chromosomes.
One sperm with 23 chromosomes and three polar bodies.
questions.why: Spermatogenesis uses equal cytokinesis after meiosis, yielding four haploid sperm; the last distractor incorrectly applies oogenesis polar-body formation to sperm production.
options: Two sperm, each with 46 chromosomes.
Four sperm, each with 46 chromosomes.
One sperm with 23 chromosomes and three polar bodies.
Four sperm, each with 23 chromosomes.

questions.stem: A population of aphids reproduces asexually, producing genetically identical offspring. A related population reproduces sexually. A new pesticide is applied. Which population is more likely to survive, and why?
questions.correct: The sexual population, because meiosis and fertilization generate varied offspring, some of which may resist the pesticide.
distractors: The asexual population, because identical offspring are uniformly resistant to the pesticide.
The asexual population, because asexual reproduction creates new mutations faster than sexual reproduction.
Neither population, because genetic variation cannot affect survival under pesticide exposure.
questions.why: Sexual reproduction produces variation that may include resistant phenotypes; the first distractor wrongly assumes identical clones are all resistant.
options: The sexual population, because meiosis and fertilization generate varied offspring, some of which may resist the pesticide.
Neither population, because genetic variation cannot affect survival under pesticide exposure.
The asexual population, because asexual reproduction creates new mutations faster than sexual reproduction.
The asexual population, because identical offspring are uniformly resistant to the pesticide.

questions.stem: In many fungi, the zygote is the only diploid cell and undergoes meiosis immediately. How does this differ from the human life cycle?
questions.correct: Fungi spend most of the life cycle haploid, while humans spend most of it diploid and grow from the zygote by mitosis.
distractors: Fungi spend most of the life cycle diploid, while humans spend most of it haploid.
Both fungi and humans have multicellular haploid and diploid stages of equal size.
Fungi produce gametes by meiosis, while humans produce gametes by mitosis.
questions.why: Fungal zygotes undergo meiosis, leaving mostly haploid stages, while human zygotes grow by mitosis into a diploid body; the last distractor swaps gamete production in the two groups.
options: Fungi spend most of the life cycle diploid, while humans spend most of it haploid.
Fungi spend most of the life cycle haploid, while humans spend most of it diploid and grow from the zygote by mitosis.
Both fungi and humans have multicellular haploid and diploid stages of equal size.
Fungi produce gametes by meiosis, while humans produce gametes by mitosis.

questions.stem: In one bivalent, a single crossover occurs between two nonsister chromatids at a point between genes A and B. After meiosis, how many of the four gametes carry a recombinant combination of A and B alleles?
questions.correct: Two of the four gametes carry a recombinant combination.
distractors: One of the four gametes carries a recombinant combination.
All four gametes carry a recombinant combination.
None of the four gametes carries a recombinant combination.
questions.why: A single crossover involves two nonsister chromatids, producing two recombinant and two parental chromatids; the all-four distractor ignores that sisters not involved remain parental.
options: One of the four gametes carries a recombinant combination.
All four gametes carry a recombinant combination.
Two of the four gametes carry a recombinant combination.
None of the four gametes carries a recombinant combination.

questions.stem: A plant cell has 2n = 12 and proceeds through meiosis. At metaphase I, how many tetrads (bivalents) line up at the cell's equatorial plane?
questions.correct: 6 tetrads, because each tetrad is one homologous pair
distractors: 12 tetrads, because each chromosome forms its own tetrad
24 tetrads, because each chromatid forms a tetrad
3 tetrads, because the chromosome number is halved first
questions.why: A tetrad is a paired set of homologs, so the count equals the haploid number n = 6; the 12 answer mistakes chromosome count for tetrad count.
options: 24 tetrads, because each chromatid forms a tetrad
12 tetrads, because each chromosome forms its own tetrad
3 tetrads, because the chromosome number is halved first
6 tetrads, because each tetrad is one homologous pair

questions.stem: A human gamete carries two copies of chromosome 7, and the two copies are identical sister chromatids with the same alleles. In which meiotic division did nondisjunction most likely occur?
questions.correct: Meiosis II, because sister chromatids failed to separate
distractors: Meiosis I, because homologous chromosomes failed to separate
Mitosis before meiosis, because the chromosome replicated twice
Fertilization, because two sperm fused with one egg
questions.why: Homologs separate in meiosis I, so identical sister chromatids reaching one gamete point to meiosis II nondisjunction; the meiosis I distractor assumes all nondisjunction happens when homologs separate.
options: Meiosis II, because sister chromatids failed to separate
Meiosis I, because homologous chromosomes failed to separate
Mitosis before meiosis, because the chromosome replicated twice
Fertilization, because two sperm fused with one egg

questions.stem: In human oogenesis, one primary oocyte produces one large ovum and smaller polar bodies. What is the main reason only one cell normally becomes the functional gamete?
questions.correct: Unequal cytokinesis concentrates cytoplasm and nutrients in one cell
distractors: Polar bodies contain the wrong number of chromosomes
Only the ovum completes DNA replication before meiosis
Polar bodies are diploid and cannot be fertilized
questions.why: Polar bodies are haploid but receive little cytoplasm and degenerate; the diploid distractor confuses small size with an abnormal chromosome number.
options: Polar bodies are diploid and cannot be fertilized
Unequal cytokinesis concentrates cytoplasm and nutrients in one cell
Only the ovum completes DNA replication before meiosis
Polar bodies contain the wrong number of chromosomes

questions.stem: During prophase I, a chiasma forms within a tetrad. Which chromatids exchange segments to produce recombinant chromosomes?
questions.correct: Nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
distractors: Sister chromatids of the same chromosome
Two chromatids from nonhomologous chromosomes
Two sister chromatids from the same homolog
questions.why: Crossing over joins nonsister chromatids from the two homologs, creating new allele combinations; exchange between sisters would not recombine different alleles.
options: Two chromatids from nonhomologous chromosomes
Two sister chromatids from the same homolog
Nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
Sister chromatids of the same chromosome

questions.stem: In a human male karyotype, the X and Y chromosomes differ in size and gene content. What happens to X and Y during meiosis I?
questions.correct: They pair as homologous chromosomes and separate to opposite poles
distractors: They fail to pair and both move to the same pole
They replicate again and form two identical X-Y pairs
They are treated as nonhomologs and assort independently of each other
questions.why: X and Y share homologous pairing regions, so they synapse and separate in meiosis I; the independent-assortment distractor wrongly treats them as unpaired nonhomologs.
options: They replicate again and form two identical X-Y pairs
They are treated as nonhomologs and assort independently of each other
They fail to pair and both move to the same pole
They pair as homologous chromosomes and separate to opposite poles

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 8 proceeds through meiosis. How many chromosomes are present in the whole cell at anaphase I and at anaphase II, respectively?
questions.correct: 8 at anaphase I and 8 at anaphase II
distractors: 8 at anaphase I and 4 at anaphase II
4 at anaphase I and 4 at anaphase II
16 at anaphase I and 8 at anaphase II
questions.why: At anaphase I homologs separate but remain in one cell; at anaphase II sister chromatids separate, doubling the chromosome count in that cell back to 8.
options: 8 at anaphase I and 8 at anaphase II
16 at anaphase I and 8 at anaphase II
8 at anaphase I and 4 at anaphase II
4 at anaphase I and 4 at anaphase II

questions.stem: A karyotype shows 46 chromosomes, but one chromosome 5 is visibly shorter than its homolog. Which conclusion is best supported by this karyotype alone?
questions.correct: A structural deletion has removed a piece of one chromosome 5
distractors: A point mutation has changed one gene on chromosome 5
The cell is haploid for chromosome 5
Nondisjunction produced an extra chromosome 5
questions.why: A karyotype resolves chromosome structure and number, so a shortened homolog indicates a deletion; the point-mutation distractor wrongly assumes karyotypes can show single-base changes.
options: A point mutation has changed one gene on chromosome 5
A structural deletion has removed a piece of one chromosome 5
The cell is haploid for chromosome 5
Nondisjunction produced an extra chromosome 5

questions.stem: A mutant cell destroys centromeric cohesin at the start of anaphase I instead of waiting until anaphase II. What is the most likely result?
questions.correct: Sister chromatids separate prematurely during meiosis I
distractors: Homologous chromosomes fail to separate during meiosis I
Crossing over occurs twice in each tetrad
The cell completes meiosis I without any chromosome segregation
questions.why: Centromeric cohesin holds sister chromatids together until meiosis II; removing it early lets sisters separate in meiosis I, while the homolog-failure distractor confuses cohesin with chiasmata.
options: Crossing over occurs twice in each tetrad
Homologous chromosomes fail to separate during meiosis I
Sister chromatids separate prematurely during meiosis I
The cell completes meiosis I without any chromosome segregation

questions.stem: A human female's primary oocytes remain arrested in prophase I until puberty. Which event has not yet occurred in these arrested cells?
questions.correct: Separation of homologous chromosomes
distractors: Replication of DNA before meiosis
Synapsis of homologous chromosomes
Crossing over between nonsister chromatids
questions.why: Prophase I arrest occurs after replication, synapsis, and crossing over but before homolog separation; the DNA-replication distractor ignores that S phase precedes the arrest.
options: Crossing over between nonsister chromatids
Synapsis of homologous chromosomes
Replication of DNA before meiosis
Separation of homologous chromosomes

questions.stem: A haploid fungus produces gametes by mitosis. Why can this haploid cell not carry out meiosis?
questions.correct: Meiosis requires homologous chromosomes to pair and segregate
distractors: Meiosis requires twice as much cytoplasm as mitosis
Haploid cells have no centromeres to attach to spindle fibers
Haploid cells cannot replicate their DNA before division
questions.why: Meiosis separates homologs, so a cell with only one set cannot perform the pairing and segregation of meiosis I; the centromere distractor confuses haploidy with loss of chromosome structures.
options: Meiosis requires homologous chromosomes to pair and segregate
Haploid cells have no centromeres to attach to spindle fibers
Haploid cells cannot replicate their DNA before division
Meiosis requires twice as much cytoplasm as mitosis

questions.stem: A human karyotype shows 45 chromosomes, including one X and no Y. Which description of this chromosome set is correct?
questions.correct: Female with monosomy X
distractors: Male with monosomy X
Female with trisomy X
Male with a normal chromosome number
questions.why: One X and no Y indicates female sex, and 45 chromosomes means one chromosome is missing; the male distractor assumes a Y must be present for male development or misreads the count.
options: Male with monosomy X
Female with monosomy X
Male with a normal chromosome number
Female with trisomy X

questions.stem: A karyotype from a human shows 47 chromosomes: two X chromosomes, one Y chromosome, and the rest autosomes. How many autosomes are present?
questions.correct: 44 autosomes
distractors: 45 autosomes
46 autosomes
22 autosomes
questions.why: Humans normally have 44 autosomes; the extra chromosome here is a sex chromosome. Counting the Y as an autosome gives 46.
options: 22 autosomes
45 autosomes
44 autosomes
46 autosomes

questions.stem: White blood cells are arrested in metaphase for karyotyping. One treated human cell contains 46 chromosomes. How many DNA molecules and centromeres are present in that cell?
questions.correct: 92 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
distractors: 46 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
92 DNA molecules and 92 centromeres
23 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
questions.why: After S phase each chromosome has two sister chromatids but one centromere, so 46 chromosomes carry 92 DNA molecules. Equating chromatids with centromeres gives 92 centromeres.
options: 46 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
92 DNA molecules and 92 centromeres
23 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
92 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres

questions.stem: A human secondary oocyte is fertilized and completes meiosis II. What chromosome content does the second polar body receive?
questions.correct: 23 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
distractors: 23 chromosomes, each with two chromatids
46 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
46 chromosomes, each with two chromatids
questions.why: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, so the second polar body gets one chromatid per chromosome. Leaving chromosomes duplicated confuses meiosis II with meiosis I.
options: 23 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
46 chromosomes, each with two chromatids
46 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
23 chromosomes, each with two chromatids

questions.stem: In one tetrad, two nonsister chromatids exchange segments in a single crossover. Before the crossover, two chromatids had paternal centromeres. How many chromatids have paternal centromeres after the crossover?
questions.why: Crossing over swaps distal segments but not centromeres, so two chromatids remain paternal. Assuming the crossover alters every chromatid gives 4.

questions.stem: A triploid plant has three homologs for each chromosome. Why does meiosis usually fail to produce balanced gametes?
questions.correct: Homologs cannot pair and segregate evenly, so gametes get variable chromosome numbers.
distractors: Sister chromatids cannot separate because centromeres do not split.
Crossing over cannot occur without exactly two homologs.
Fertilization cannot occur because the plant's gametes are diploid.
questions.why: Meiosis requires homologs to pair and separate; an odd number leaves unpaired chromosomes and uneven segregation. Blaming DNA replication rather than homolog pairing is a common substitution.
options: Sister chromatids cannot separate because centromeres do not split.
Crossing over cannot occur without exactly two homologs.
Homologs cannot pair and segregate evenly, so gametes get variable chromosome numbers.
Fertilization cannot occur because the plant's gametes are diploid.

questions.stem: In a mutant cell with 2n = 8, meiosis I chromosome segregation is normal, but cytokinesis after meiosis I fails. What is the immediate result?
questions.correct: One cell containing two haploid nuclei, each with 4 chromosomes.
distractors: One diploid nucleus with 8 chromosomes.
Two haploid cells, each with 4 chromosomes.
Four haploid nuclei, each with 2 chromosomes.
questions.why: Chromosomes segregate into two haploid nuclei, but the cell does not divide, so both nuclei remain in one cell. The two-cell result describes normal cytokinesis.
options: Four haploid nuclei, each with 2 chromosomes.
One diploid nucleus with 8 chromosomes.
Two haploid cells, each with 4 chromosomes.
One cell containing two haploid nuclei, each with 4 chromosomes.

questions.stem: A human spermatogonium undergoes one mitotic division, and both daughter cells immediately complete meiosis. How many sperm are produced?
questions.correct: 8 sperm
distractors: 4 sperm
2 sperm
16 sperm
questions.why: One spermatogonium gives two primary spermatocytes, and each primary spermatocyte yields four sperm. Forgetting the mitotic division gives 4; doubling twice gives 16.
options: 8 sperm
2 sperm
4 sperm
16 sperm

questions.stem: A mutant prevents cleavage of cohesin along chromosome arms in meiosis I but leaves centromeric cohesin protected normally. What is the most likely result?
questions.correct: Homologs remain joined and fail to separate in anaphase I.
distractors: Sister chromatids separate prematurely in anaphase I.
Crossing over occurs twice as often.
Meiosis II is skipped entirely.
questions.why: Arm cohesin holds homologs together until anaphase I; without its cleavage, homologs cannot separate. The premature-sister result confuses arm cohesin with centromeric cohesin.
options: Sister chromatids separate prematurely in anaphase I.
Homologs remain joined and fail to separate in anaphase I.
Meiosis II is skipped entirely.
Crossing over occurs twice as often.

questions.stem: A human zygote has 47 chromosomes, including three X chromosomes and no Y. The sperm that fertilized it carried one X. What chromosome content did the egg have?
questions.correct: 23 chromosomes, including two X chromosomes.
distractors: 23 chromosomes, including one X chromosome.
24 chromosomes, including one X chromosome.
23 chromosomes, including no X chromosome.
questions.why: The zygote's extra X must have come from the egg, so the egg carried 22 autosomes plus two X chromosomes. An egg with one X would produce a 46,XX zygote.
options: 23 chromosomes, including no X chromosome.
24 chromosomes, including one X chromosome.
23 chromosomes, including two X chromosomes.
23 chromosomes, including one X chromosome.

questions.stem: A human egg with 24 chromosomes is fertilized by a sperm with 22 chromosomes. The zygote has 46 chromosomes. Why is it still considered aneuploid?
questions.correct: It has an extra copy of one chromosome and is missing another, so the set is unbalanced.
distractors: It has 46 chromosomes, so it is a normal diploid.
It is triploid because three chromosome sets are present.
It is haploid because both gametes were abnormal.
questions.why: Aneuploidy is an abnormal chromosome set, not just an abnormal total; the extra and missing chromosomes unbalance the zygote. Counting total chromosomes only would call it normal diploid.
options: It is triploid because three chromosome sets are present.
It has 46 chromosomes, so it is a normal diploid.
It is haploid because both gametes were abnormal.
It has an extra copy of one chromosome and is missing another, so the set is unbalanced.

questions.stem: A drug prevents spindle formation during meiosis II of a fertilized human secondary oocyte. What is the most direct consequence?
questions.correct: Sister chromatids cannot separate, so a haploid ovum and second polar body cannot form.
distractors: Homologs fail to separate, so the oocyte remains diploid.
Crossing over occurs twice as often in prophase II.
The zygote immediately becomes triploid.
questions.why: Meiosis II uses a spindle to separate sister chromatids; without it, the ovum and polar body are not produced. The homolog-separation result confuses meiosis II with meiosis I.
options: Sister chromatids cannot separate, so a haploid ovum and second polar body cannot form.
The zygote immediately becomes triploid.
Homologs fail to separate, so the oocyte remains diploid.
Crossing over occurs twice as often in prophase II.

questions.stem: A human karyotype shows 23 pairs of chromosomes. Which statement about that display is correct?
options: Twenty-two pairs are autosomes, and the members of a pair are homologs matched in length, shape and gene loci, one inherited from each parent.
All 23 pairs are autosomes, and each pair is a set of sister chromatids.
Twenty-three pairs of autosomes are present plus a separate pair of sex chromosomes.
The pairing proves the cell is haploid, because each chromosome has one partner.
questions.why: Humans carry 22 autosome pairs plus one sex pair; homologs match in length and shape and carry the same loci, one copy per parent.

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 6 has finished meiosis I and its two daughters are at metaphase II. How many chromosomes and chromatids does each daughter hold?
options: 6 chromosomes and 6 chromatids, because the set has not been halved yet.
3 chromosomes and 6 chromatids, because each chromosome is still two sister chromatids.
3 chromosomes and 3 chromatids, because the sisters have already separated.
6 chromosomes and 12 chromatids, because the DNA was copied after meiosis I.
questions.why: Meiosis I halves the set to n = 3 but leaves each chromosome doubled, so 3 chromosomes carry 6 chromatids until anaphase II.

questions.stem: At metaphase II, the two sister chromatids of a chromosome attach to microtubules from opposite poles. Why are those sisters not genetically identical?
options: Because DNA replication in meiosis II introduces new mutations into one sister.
Because the sisters separated during anaphase I and then rejoined.
Because crossing over in prophase I exchanged segments between nonsister chromatids, so the sisters carry different allele combinations.
Because maternal and paternal chromosomes fused at the metaphase II plate.
questions.why: Crossing over exchanges corresponding segments between nonsister chromatids in prophase I, so each sister carries a mixed set of alleles.

questions.stem: During anaphase I the homologs separate while sister chromatids stay together. What makes that possible?
options: Cohesin is cleaved at the centromeres first, then along the arms in anaphase II.
Cohesin is not involved; the spindle pulls homologs apart directly.
Cohesin is fully degraded at the end of metaphase I, releasing sisters immediately.
Cohesin is cleaved along the chromosome arms, while centromeric cohesin stays intact until anaphase II.
questions.why: Arm cohesin is cut in anaphase I to free the homologs; centromeric cohesin persists so sisters travel together until anaphase II.

questions.stem: Why is there no DNA replication between meiosis I and meiosis II?
options: Because the chromosomes were already replicated in interphase, and a second replication would double the genome again.
Because meiosis II is not a real division and requires no new DNA.
Because replication happens during telophase I and is too fast to observe.
Because each daughter cell replicates its DNA during prophase II.
questions.why: One S phase precedes meiosis I; replicating again before meiosis II would give each gamete twice the DNA it should carry.

questions.stem: Why are all four products of meiosis genetically distinct from one another?
options: Because each product receives a different number of chromosomes.
Independent assortment gives different combinations of homologs, and crossing over puts different alleles on the chromatids.
Because mutation occurs in every one of the four daughter cells.
Because sister chromatids are identical and separate randomly at anaphase II.
questions.why: Assortment mixes which homologs travel together and crossing over mixes alleles along each chromosome, so no two products match.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly states what separates in each meiotic anaphase?
options: Anaphase I separates sister chromatids; anaphase II separates homologs.
Both anaphases separate homologs, which is why the set halves twice.
Anaphase I separates homologous chromosomes; anaphase II separates sister chromatids.
Anaphase I separates sister chromatids of each homolog simultaneously.
questions.why: Meiosis I is the reductional division that pulls homologs apart; meiosis II is the equational division that splits sisters.

questions.stem: Two homologous pairs line up at metaphase I. What does independent assortment predict about the resulting gametes?
options: Only two gamete types are possible, because the pairs travel together.
Gametes carry both homologs of each pair until meiosis II.
Two gamete types form, with the recombinant types appearing only after crossing over.
Four gamete types are possible, because each pair's orientation is independent of the other pair's.
questions.why: Each pair orients randomly and independently, so two pairs produce 2^2 = 4 equally likely gamete combinations.

questions.stem: What happens during synapsis in prophase I?
options: Homologs pair along their lengths, held by the synaptonemal complex, and nonsister chromatids exchange corresponding segments.
Sister chromatids separate at the centromere and begin moving to the poles.
Homologs line up single file at the metaphase plate.
The nuclear envelope re-forms around each haploid set.
questions.why: Synapsis is the physical pairing of homologs in prophase I; crossing over occurs within that paired structure and creates chiasmata.

questions.stem: A chromosome in a gamete carries alleles that came from both of the student's grandparents on the same side of the family. What produced that?
options: Independent assortment at metaphase I, which mixes whole chromosomes.
Crossing over between nonsister chromatids in prophase I, which makes recombinant chromosomes.
Random fertilization, which combines gametes from two parents.
Nondisjunction, which changes how chromosomes are distributed.
questions.why: A single chromosome carrying DNA from both homologs is the signature of crossing over; assortment only mixes intact chromosomes.

questions.stem: The number of gamete combinations from independent assortment is 2^n, where n is the haploid number. For humans, what does that give?
options: 2^46, more than 70 trillion combinations.
23^2, or 529 combinations.
2^23, more than 8 million combinations.
2 x 23, or 46 combinations.
questions.why: n = 23 in humans, so independent assortment alone yields 2^23, about 8.4 million different gametes.

questions.stem: Why does random fertilization increase variation even though it adds no new alleles?
options: Because fertilization creates new alleles by recombining DNA inside the zygote.
Because the sperm selects which of the egg's chromosomes will be retained.
Because fertilization doubles the chromosome number of each gamete.
Because any sperm can fuse with any ovum, so the combination of two already-varied gametes multiplies the possibilities.
questions.why: Fertilization does not create alleles; it pairs one of millions of sperm with one of millions of eggs, multiplying combinations.

questions.stem: One primary spermatocyte yields four sperm with 24, 24, 22 and 22 chromosomes (human). Which division failed?
options: Meiosis I, because all four gametes are abnormal and the error appears in both products of the first division.
Meiosis II, because only one of the two secondary cells produced abnormal gametes.
Mitosis after fertilization, because the counts are unequal.
Crossing over, because recombination changed the chromosome counts.
questions.why: A meiosis I nondisjunction sends both homologs to one pole, so both secondary cells inherit the error and all four gametes are abnormal.

questions.stem: Four gametes carry 24, 22, 23 and 23 chromosomes. Which event explains this pattern?
options: Nondisjunction in meiosis I, because all four products differ from 23.
Nondisjunction in meiosis II, because only one of the two secondary cells divided abnormally.
Failure of crossing over, because recombination preserves the count.
Failure of cytokinesis in meiosis I, because the cells never separated.
questions.why: When exactly two of four gametes are abnormal and the other two are normal, the error was confined to one secondary cell at meiosis II.

questions.stem: An n+1 gamete fuses with a normal n gamete. What is the result, and how does it differ from an n-1 gamete fusing?
options: A monosomic zygote; an n-1 gamete gives trisomy, which is usually viable.
A haploid zygote; an n-1 gamete gives a diploid zygote.
A trisomic zygote with three copies of one chromosome; an n-1 gamete gives monosomy, which is usually lethal.
A polyploid zygote with two extra sets; an n-1 gamete removes one whole set.
questions.why: n+1 plus n gives three copies (trisomy, as in trisomy 21); n-1 plus n leaves one copy (monosomy), which is usually not viable.

questions.stem: A sperm carries a Y chromosome. What follows for the zygote, and what was the sperm's own chromosome content?
options: The zygote will be XX and female, and the sperm carried two diploid sets.
The zygote will be XY and male, and the sperm carried 46 chromosomes.
The zygote's sex cannot be predicted, because the egg may also carry a Y.
The zygote will be XY and male, and the sperm carried a single haploid set of 23.
questions.why: Eggs always carry X, so a Y-bearing sperm produces an XY male; gametes are haploid, carrying 23 chromosomes.

questions.stem: Which statement about gametes in animals is correct?
options: They are the only haploid cells, and they do not divide again before fertilization.
They are diploid, and they divide by mitosis after meiosis.
They are haploid and divide by meiosis a second time before fusing.
They are haploid in males but diploid in females.
questions.why: Gametes are the sole haploid cells in animals; they fuse rather than divide, and the zygote then grows by mitosis.

questions.stem: Two chromosomes form a homologous pair. Which description is correct?
options: They carry identical alleles at every locus, which is why they pair.
They carry the same genes at the same loci, matched in length and shape, but may carry different alleles.
They carry different genes entirely, and pairing matches them by size only.
They are the two sister chromatids produced when the chromosome replicated.
questions.why: Homologs share loci and structure, one from each parent; the alleles at those loci can differ, which is what makes crossing over matter.

questions.stem: Which set of events occurs in meiosis but never in mitosis?
options: Chromosome condensation, spindle formation and sister chromatid separation.
DNA replication in interphase and cytokinesis at the end of division.
Synapsis with crossing over in prophase I, homologous pairs at the metaphase plate, and homolog separation in anaphase I.
Nuclear envelope breakdown and kinetochore attachment to microtubules.
questions.why: Those three events are the reason meiosis reduces the set; everything else on the list is shared machinery.

questions.stem: What do haploid and diploid actually describe?
options: The number of chromatids per chromosome, one versus two.
The amount of DNA in the nucleus, 2C versus 4C.
Whether the cell is a gamete or a somatic cell, regardless of chromosome number.
The number of chromosome SETS: one of each chromosome versus two of each.
questions.why: Diploid means two sets and haploid means one set; a replicated haploid cell still has two chromatids per chromosome, which is a different measure.

questions.stem: A human gamete carries 23 chromosomes. What is that set, and what happens to the number at fertilization?
options: 22 autosomes plus 1 sex chromosome, and fertilization restores 2n = 46.
22 autosomes plus 1 sex chromosome, and fertilization restores 2n = 23.
23 autosomes plus 1 sex chromosome, and fertilization gives 48.
46 chromosomes, half of which are degraded at fertilization.
questions.why: n = 23 means 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome; adding the other gamete's set gives 46, the diploid number.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of crossing an individual of unknown genotype to a homozygous recessive partner?
options: It doubles the number of offspring, which makes ratios easier to read.
The recessive partner contributes only recessive alleles, so the offspring phenotypes reveal the unknown genotype.
It converts recessive alleles into dominant ones in the offspring.
It prevents crossing over, so linkage can be measured directly.
questions.why: Because the tester contributes only recessive alleles, any dominant offspring must have received the dominant allele from the unknown parent.

questions.stem: A tall pea plant is crossed with a dwarf plant (tt), and all 80 offspring are tall. What is the best conclusion?
options: The tall parent is heterozygous (Tt), because half the offspring should be dwarf.
The tall parent's genotype cannot be determined from any offspring counts.
The tall parent is homozygous dominant (TT), because no recessive offspring appeared.
The cross shows that height and flower color are linked.
questions.why: A heterozygote crossed to tt yields roughly 1:1; with 80 offspring all dominant, the parent is almost certainly TT.

questions.stem: A double heterozygote is testcrossed and yields four phenotypic classes in roughly equal numbers. What does that establish?
options: The two genes are completely linked, which is why all four classes appear.
One gene is epistatic to the other, which masks one class.
The parent was homozygous for both traits, which is why the ratio is even.
The two genes assort independently, which is why the 1:1:1:1 ratio appears.
questions.why: Equal numbers of all four classes is the signature of independent assortment; complete linkage would keep only the two parental classes.

questions.stem: Two heterozygotes for unlinked genes are crossed. What offspring ratio is expected?
options: 9:3:3:1 across the four phenotype combinations.
1:1:1:1, because each gene assorts independently.
3:1, because only one gene is segregating.
1:2:1, because each genotype appears once.
questions.why: A 9:3:3:1 ratio is the product of two independent 3:1 monohybrid ratios.

questions.stem: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what does the frequency of the recessive PHENOTYPE give you directly?
options: q, which you square to get the recessive allele frequency.
q^2, which you square-root to get the recessive allele frequency q.
2pq, which you halve to get the heterozygote frequency.
p^2, which you subtract from 1 to get q.
questions.why: Only recessive homozygotes show the recessive phenotype, so their frequency is q^2; rooting it gives q.

questions.stem: In a population at equilibrium, 16 percent of individuals show the recessive phenotype. What fraction is heterozygous?
options: 0.16, because the recessive phenotype frequency equals the heterozygote frequency.
0.24, because q times p gives the heterozygote fraction.
0.36, because p squared gives the heterozygote fraction.
questions.why: q^2 = 0.16 gives q = 0.4 and p = 0.6, so heterozygotes = 2(0.6)(0.4) = 0.48.

questions.stem: A beetle population of 1,000 is reduced to 20 individuals on an isolated island. Which assumption of Hardy-Weinberg is most likely to fail first?
options: Random mating, because small populations always mate assortatively.
No mutation, because small populations mutate more often per individual.
No gene flow, because islands cannot exchange migrants at all.
Large population size, because allele frequencies shift by chance in a small population.
questions.why: Genetic drift is the consequence of small N: sampling error moves allele frequencies regardless of fitness.

questions.stem: What does it mean for a population to be at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
options: Allele and genotype frequencies stay constant from generation to generation because no evolutionary force is acting.
Every individual has the same genotype, so no variation remains.
The dominant allele is being selected for, so its frequency rises.
Mutation and selection are exactly balanced, holding the recessive allele constant.
questions.why: Equilibrium means the frequencies are stable; it is the null model against which real change is measured.

questions.stem: What is the correct division of labor between mutation and sexual reproduction?
options: Meiosis creates new alleles; mutation only redistributes them among offspring.
Mutation originates new alleles; meiosis and fertilization redistribute the alleles that already exist.
Both create new alleles, which is why sexual populations mutate faster.
Neither creates variation; variation comes only from the environment.
questions.why: Mutation is the only source of new alleles; assortment, crossing over and fertilization reshuffle them into new combinations.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches a source of variation to its stage?
options: Independent assortment in prophase I, crossing over at metaphase I, mutation at fertilization.
Crossing over in anaphase I, independent assortment at anaphase II, mutation at fusion.
Crossing over in prophase I, independent assortment at metaphase I, random fertilization at fusion.
Random fertilization in prophase I, crossing over at metaphase II, assortment at fusion.
questions.why: Crossing over is a prophase I event, assortment happens as pairs orient at metaphase I, and fertilization combines two gametes.

questions.stem: A human cell reaches the end of telophase I. What does each daughter cell contain?
options: 46 chromosomes, each made of one chromatid, so the cell is still diploid.
23 chromosomes, each made of one chromatid, so the cell is already a gamete.
46 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids, so 92 chromatids in total.
23 chromosomes, each still made of two sister chromatids, so 46 chromatids in a haploid cell.
questions.why: Meiosis I halves the set to 23 but does not split centromeres, so each chromosome is still doubled until anaphase II.

questions.stem: Why does a sexual life cycle require both meiosis and fertilization?
options: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and fertilization restores it, so the number stays constant across generations.
Meiosis restores the chromosome number and fertilization halves it before development.
Both halve the number, so the zygote begins with a quarter of the parental set.
Fertilization alone is sufficient; meiosis exists only to make gametes smaller.
questions.why: Without halving, each generation would double the genome; without fusion, the set could never be restored.

questions.stem: A karyotype from a human fetus shows 47 chromosomes, including three copies of chromosome 21 and two X chromosomes. Which description of this chromosome set is correct?
questions.correct: 45 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes, with the extra chromosome being an autosome.
distractors: 44 autosomes and 3 sex chromosomes, with the extra chromosome being a sex chromosome.
47 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes, with no sex chromosomes counted separately.
45 autosomes and 1 sex chromosome, with one X chromosome missing.
questions.why: The 47 chromosomes split into 45 autosomes plus 2 X sex chromosomes, and chromosome 21 is an autosome; the first distractor wrongly counts the extra copy as a sex chromosome.
options: 45 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes, with the extra chromosome being an autosome.
47 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes, with no sex chromosomes counted separately.
45 autosomes and 1 sex chromosome, with one X chromosome missing.
44 autosomes and 3 sex chromosomes, with the extra chromosome being a sex chromosome.

questions.stem: To make a karyotype, a technician arrests white blood cells in metaphase with a drug that prevents spindle fibers from separating chromosomes. Why does metaphase make homologs easiest to pair?
questions.correct: Chromosomes are condensed and still duplicated, so homologs can be matched by size, centromere position, and banding.
distractors: Homologs have already separated, so each chromosome can be compared with its partner independently.
Crossing over is complete, so recombinant chromosomes can be identified by their new banding patterns.
DNA is replicating, so each homolog is present as a single chromatid that can be aligned.
questions.why: At metaphase chromosomes are condensed with sister chromatids still attached, allowing homologs to be paired; the first distractor confuses metaphase with anaphase separation.
options: Homologs have already separated, so each chromosome can be compared with its partner independently.
Chromosomes are condensed and still duplicated, so homologs can be matched by size, centromere position, and banding.
DNA is replicating, so each homolog is present as a single chromatid that can be aligned.
Crossing over is complete, so recombinant chromosomes can be identified by their new banding patterns.

questions.stem: A karyotype from a healthy person shows 46 chromosomes with no visible structural abnormalities. What can be concluded from the karyotype alone?
questions.correct: No chromosome-number or large structural abnormality was detected, but a single-gene mutation could still be present.
distractors: The person cannot carry any recessive alleles because both homologs look normal.
All alleles on the person's homologous chromosomes must be identical.
Crossing over did not occur during the meiosis that produced the person's gametes.
questions.why: A karyotype detects chromosome number and large structure, not allele sequences; the second distractor wrongly equates homologous chromosomes with identical alleles.
options: The person cannot carry any recessive alleles because both homologs look normal.
Crossing over did not occur during the meiosis that produced the person's gametes.
No chromosome-number or large structural abnormality was detected, but a single-gene mutation could still be present.
All alleles on the person's homologous chromosomes must be identical.

questions.stem: A human secondary oocyte is released at ovulation and is then fertilized. What completes meiosis II, and what cells are produced?
questions.correct: Sperm entry triggers completion, producing one ovum and a second polar body.
distractors: Ovulation triggers completion, producing four ova from the secondary oocyte.
Meiosis II completes before fertilization, producing two ova from the secondary oocyte.
Fertilization blocks meiosis II, so the first polar body becomes the ovum.
questions.why: The secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase II and completes only after sperm entry, with unequal cytokinesis yielding one ovum and a polar body; the first distractor assumes four ova.
options: Meiosis II completes before fertilization, producing two ova from the secondary oocyte.
Ovulation triggers completion, producing four ova from the secondary oocyte.
Fertilization blocks meiosis II, so the first polar body becomes the ovum.
Sperm entry triggers completion, producing one ovum and a second polar body.

questions.stem: In a moss, the green leafy gametophyte is haploid and produces gametes, while the diploid sporophyte produces spores. Which statement correctly explains how these cells are made?
questions.correct: The haploid gametophyte makes gametes by mitosis, and the diploid sporophyte makes spores by meiosis.
distractors: The haploid gametophyte makes gametes by meiosis, and the diploid sporophyte makes spores by mitosis.
Both gametes and spores are made by meiosis because both are haploid cells.
Both gametes and spores are made by mitosis because both are single cells.
questions.why: Mitosis in an already haploid gametophyte preserves n, while meiosis in the diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores; the second distractor assumes any haploid product requires meiosis.
options: The haploid gametophyte makes gametes by mitosis, and the diploid sporophyte makes spores by meiosis.
The haploid gametophyte makes gametes by meiosis, and the diploid sporophyte makes spores by mitosis.
Both gametes and spores are made by meiosis because both are haploid cells.
Both gametes and spores are made by mitosis because both are single cells.

questions.stem: A human zygote with 46 chromosomes divides repeatedly to form an embryo, and later some adult gonadal cells undergo meiosis. Which pairing correctly describes the two divisions?
questions.correct: Mitosis maintains the diploid number in body cells, while meiosis halves it to produce haploid gametes.
distractors: Mitosis halves the chromosome number, while meiosis doubles it before fertilization.
Both divisions reduce the chromosome number by half in each daughter cell.
Meiosis maintains the diploid number in body cells, while mitosis produces gametes.
questions.why: Mitosis supports growth with the same diploid set, and meiosis produces haploid gametes; the third distractor swaps the roles of the two divisions.
options: Meiosis maintains the diploid number in body cells, while mitosis produces gametes.
Mitosis maintains the diploid number in body cells, while meiosis halves it to produce haploid gametes.
Both divisions reduce the chromosome number by half in each daughter cell.
Mitosis halves the chromosome number, while meiosis doubles it before fertilization.

questions.stem: At metaphase I, a human cell has 23 bivalents, or tetrads. What does each bivalent contain?
questions.correct: Two homologous chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, for four chromatids total.
distractors: Two sister chromatids from one chromosome, for two chromatids total.
Four homologous chromosomes, each with one chromatid, for four chromosomes total.
One autosome and one sex chromosome, for two chromosomes total.
questions.why: A bivalent is a paired homologous pair, and each homolog is duplicated, giving four chromatids; the first distractor confuses sister chromatids with homologs.
options: Two sister chromatids from one chromosome, for two chromatids total.
One autosome and one sex chromosome, for two chromosomes total.
Two homologous chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, for four chromatids total.
Four homologous chromosomes, each with one chromatid, for four chromosomes total.

questions.stem: A human primary spermatocyte with 46 chromosomes completes meiosis and cytokinesis normally. How many sperm are produced, and what chromosome number does each carry?
questions.correct: Four sperm, each with 23 chromosomes.
distractors: Two sperm, each with 46 chromosomes.
Four sperm, each with 46 chromosomes.
One sperm with 23 chromosomes and three polar bodies.
questions.why: Spermatogenesis uses equal cytokinesis after meiosis, yielding four haploid sperm; the last distractor incorrectly applies oogenesis polar-body formation to sperm production.
options: Two sperm, each with 46 chromosomes.
Four sperm, each with 46 chromosomes.
One sperm with 23 chromosomes and three polar bodies.
Four sperm, each with 23 chromosomes.

questions.stem: A population of aphids reproduces asexually, producing genetically identical offspring. A related population reproduces sexually. A new pesticide is applied. Which population is more likely to survive, and why?
questions.correct: The sexual population, because meiosis and fertilization generate varied offspring, some of which may resist the pesticide.
distractors: The asexual population, because identical offspring are uniformly resistant to the pesticide.
The asexual population, because asexual reproduction creates new mutations faster than sexual reproduction.
Neither population, because genetic variation cannot affect survival under pesticide exposure.
questions.why: Sexual reproduction produces variation that may include resistant phenotypes; the first distractor wrongly assumes identical clones are all resistant.
options: The sexual population, because meiosis and fertilization generate varied offspring, some of which may resist the pesticide.
Neither population, because genetic variation cannot affect survival under pesticide exposure.
The asexual population, because asexual reproduction creates new mutations faster than sexual reproduction.
The asexual population, because identical offspring are uniformly resistant to the pesticide.

questions.stem: In many fungi, the zygote is the only diploid cell and undergoes meiosis immediately. How does this differ from the human life cycle?
questions.correct: Fungi spend most of the life cycle haploid, while humans spend most of it diploid and grow from the zygote by mitosis.
distractors: Fungi spend most of the life cycle diploid, while humans spend most of it haploid.
Both fungi and humans have multicellular haploid and diploid stages of equal size.
Fungi produce gametes by meiosis, while humans produce gametes by mitosis.
questions.why: Fungal zygotes undergo meiosis, leaving mostly haploid stages, while human zygotes grow by mitosis into a diploid body; the last distractor swaps gamete production in the two groups.
options: Fungi spend most of the life cycle diploid, while humans spend most of it haploid.
Fungi spend most of the life cycle haploid, while humans spend most of it diploid and grow from the zygote by mitosis.
Both fungi and humans have multicellular haploid and diploid stages of equal size.
Fungi produce gametes by meiosis, while humans produce gametes by mitosis.

questions.stem: In one bivalent, a single crossover occurs between two nonsister chromatids at a point between genes A and B. After meiosis, how many of the four gametes carry a recombinant combination of A and B alleles?
questions.correct: Two of the four gametes carry a recombinant combination.
distractors: One of the four gametes carries a recombinant combination.
All four gametes carry a recombinant combination.
None of the four gametes carries a recombinant combination.
questions.why: A single crossover involves two nonsister chromatids, producing two recombinant and two parental chromatids; the all-four distractor ignores that sisters not involved remain parental.
options: One of the four gametes carries a recombinant combination.
All four gametes carry a recombinant combination.
Two of the four gametes carry a recombinant combination.
None of the four gametes carries a recombinant combination.

questions.stem: A plant cell has 2n = 12 and proceeds through meiosis. At metaphase I, how many tetrads (bivalents) line up at the cell's equatorial plane?
questions.correct: 6 tetrads, because each tetrad is one homologous pair
distractors: 12 tetrads, because each chromosome forms its own tetrad
24 tetrads, because each chromatid forms a tetrad
3 tetrads, because the chromosome number is halved first
questions.why: A tetrad is a paired set of homologs, so the count equals the haploid number n = 6; the 12 answer mistakes chromosome count for tetrad count.
options: 24 tetrads, because each chromatid forms a tetrad
12 tetrads, because each chromosome forms its own tetrad
3 tetrads, because the chromosome number is halved first
6 tetrads, because each tetrad is one homologous pair

questions.stem: A human gamete carries two copies of chromosome 7, and the two copies are identical sister chromatids with the same alleles. In which meiotic division did nondisjunction most likely occur?
questions.correct: Meiosis II, because sister chromatids failed to separate
distractors: Meiosis I, because homologous chromosomes failed to separate
Mitosis before meiosis, because the chromosome replicated twice
Fertilization, because two sperm fused with one egg
questions.why: Homologs separate in meiosis I, so identical sister chromatids reaching one gamete point to meiosis II nondisjunction; the meiosis I distractor assumes all nondisjunction happens when homologs separate.
options: Meiosis II, because sister chromatids failed to separate
Meiosis I, because homologous chromosomes failed to separate
Mitosis before meiosis, because the chromosome replicated twice
Fertilization, because two sperm fused with one egg

questions.stem: In human oogenesis, one primary oocyte produces one large ovum and smaller polar bodies. What is the main reason only one cell normally becomes the functional gamete?
questions.correct: Unequal cytokinesis concentrates cytoplasm and nutrients in one cell
distractors: Polar bodies contain the wrong number of chromosomes
Only the ovum completes DNA replication before meiosis
Polar bodies are diploid and cannot be fertilized
questions.why: Polar bodies are haploid but receive little cytoplasm and degenerate; the diploid distractor confuses small size with an abnormal chromosome number.
options: Polar bodies are diploid and cannot be fertilized
Unequal cytokinesis concentrates cytoplasm and nutrients in one cell
Only the ovum completes DNA replication before meiosis
Polar bodies contain the wrong number of chromosomes

questions.stem: During prophase I, a chiasma forms within a tetrad. Which chromatids exchange segments to produce recombinant chromosomes?
questions.correct: Nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
distractors: Sister chromatids of the same chromosome
Two chromatids from nonhomologous chromosomes
Two sister chromatids from the same homolog
questions.why: Crossing over joins nonsister chromatids from the two homologs, creating new allele combinations; exchange between sisters would not recombine different alleles.
options: Two chromatids from nonhomologous chromosomes
Two sister chromatids from the same homolog
Nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
Sister chromatids of the same chromosome

questions.stem: In a human male karyotype, the X and Y chromosomes differ in size and gene content. What happens to X and Y during meiosis I?
questions.correct: They pair as homologous chromosomes and separate to opposite poles
distractors: They fail to pair and both move to the same pole
They replicate again and form two identical X-Y pairs
They are treated as nonhomologs and assort independently of each other
questions.why: X and Y share homologous pairing regions, so they synapse and separate in meiosis I; the independent-assortment distractor wrongly treats them as unpaired nonhomologs.
options: They replicate again and form two identical X-Y pairs
They are treated as nonhomologs and assort independently of each other
They fail to pair and both move to the same pole
They pair as homologous chromosomes and separate to opposite poles

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 8 proceeds through meiosis. How many chromosomes are present in the whole cell at anaphase I and at anaphase II, respectively?
questions.correct: 8 at anaphase I and 8 at anaphase II
distractors: 8 at anaphase I and 4 at anaphase II
4 at anaphase I and 4 at anaphase II
16 at anaphase I and 8 at anaphase II
questions.why: At anaphase I homologs separate but remain in one cell; at anaphase II sister chromatids separate, doubling the chromosome count in that cell back to 8.
options: 8 at anaphase I and 8 at anaphase II
16 at anaphase I and 8 at anaphase II
8 at anaphase I and 4 at anaphase II
4 at anaphase I and 4 at anaphase II

questions.stem: A karyotype shows 46 chromosomes, but one chromosome 5 is visibly shorter than its homolog. Which conclusion is best supported by this karyotype alone?
questions.correct: A structural deletion has removed a piece of one chromosome 5
distractors: A point mutation has changed one gene on chromosome 5
The cell is haploid for chromosome 5
Nondisjunction produced an extra chromosome 5
questions.why: A karyotype resolves chromosome structure and number, so a shortened homolog indicates a deletion; the point-mutation distractor wrongly assumes karyotypes can show single-base changes.
options: A point mutation has changed one gene on chromosome 5
A structural deletion has removed a piece of one chromosome 5
The cell is haploid for chromosome 5
Nondisjunction produced an extra chromosome 5

questions.stem: A mutant cell destroys centromeric cohesin at the start of anaphase I instead of waiting until anaphase II. What is the most likely result?
questions.correct: Sister chromatids separate prematurely during meiosis I
distractors: Homologous chromosomes fail to separate during meiosis I
Crossing over occurs twice in each tetrad
The cell completes meiosis I without any chromosome segregation
questions.why: Centromeric cohesin holds sister chromatids together until meiosis II; removing it early lets sisters separate in meiosis I, while the homolog-failure distractor confuses cohesin with chiasmata.
options: Crossing over occurs twice in each tetrad
Homologous chromosomes fail to separate during meiosis I
Sister chromatids separate prematurely during meiosis I
The cell completes meiosis I without any chromosome segregation

questions.stem: A human female's primary oocytes remain arrested in prophase I until puberty. Which event has not yet occurred in these arrested cells?
questions.correct: Separation of homologous chromosomes
distractors: Replication of DNA before meiosis
Synapsis of homologous chromosomes
Crossing over between nonsister chromatids
questions.why: Prophase I arrest occurs after replication, synapsis, and crossing over but before homolog separation; the DNA-replication distractor ignores that S phase precedes the arrest.
options: Crossing over between nonsister chromatids
Synapsis of homologous chromosomes
Replication of DNA before meiosis
Separation of homologous chromosomes

questions.stem: A haploid fungus produces gametes by mitosis. Why can this haploid cell not carry out meiosis?
questions.correct: Meiosis requires homologous chromosomes to pair and segregate
distractors: Meiosis requires twice as much cytoplasm as mitosis
Haploid cells have no centromeres to attach to spindle fibers
Haploid cells cannot replicate their DNA before division
questions.why: Meiosis separates homologs, so a cell with only one set cannot perform the pairing and segregation of meiosis I; the centromere distractor confuses haploidy with loss of chromosome structures.
options: Meiosis requires homologous chromosomes to pair and segregate
Haploid cells have no centromeres to attach to spindle fibers
Haploid cells cannot replicate their DNA before division
Meiosis requires twice as much cytoplasm as mitosis

questions.stem: A human karyotype shows 45 chromosomes, including one X and no Y. Which description of this chromosome set is correct?
questions.correct: Female with monosomy X
distractors: Male with monosomy X
Female with trisomy X
Male with a normal chromosome number
questions.why: One X and no Y indicates female sex, and 45 chromosomes means one chromosome is missing; the male distractor assumes a Y must be present for male development or misreads the count.
options: Male with monosomy X
Female with monosomy X
Male with a normal chromosome number
Female with trisomy X

questions.stem: A karyotype from a human shows 47 chromosomes: two X chromosomes, one Y chromosome, and the rest autosomes. How many autosomes are present?
questions.correct: 44 autosomes
distractors: 45 autosomes
46 autosomes
22 autosomes
questions.why: Humans normally have 44 autosomes; the extra chromosome here is a sex chromosome. Counting the Y as an autosome gives 46.
options: 22 autosomes
45 autosomes
44 autosomes
46 autosomes

questions.stem: White blood cells are arrested in metaphase for karyotyping. One treated human cell contains 46 chromosomes. How many DNA molecules and centromeres are present in that cell?
questions.correct: 92 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
distractors: 46 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
92 DNA molecules and 92 centromeres
23 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
questions.why: After S phase each chromosome has two sister chromatids but one centromere, so 46 chromosomes carry 92 DNA molecules. Equating chromatids with centromeres gives 92 centromeres.
options: 46 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
92 DNA molecules and 92 centromeres
23 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
92 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres

questions.stem: A human secondary oocyte is fertilized and completes meiosis II. What chromosome content does the second polar body receive?
questions.correct: 23 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
distractors: 23 chromosomes, each with two chromatids
46 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
46 chromosomes, each with two chromatids
questions.why: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, so the second polar body gets one chromatid per chromosome. Leaving chromosomes duplicated confuses meiosis II with meiosis I.
options: 23 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
46 chromosomes, each with two chromatids
46 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
23 chromosomes, each with two chromatids

questions.stem: In one tetrad, two nonsister chromatids exchange segments in a single crossover. Before the crossover, two chromatids had paternal centromeres. How many chromatids have paternal centromeres after the crossover?
questions.why: Crossing over swaps distal segments but not centromeres, so two chromatids remain paternal. Assuming the crossover alters every chromatid gives 4.

questions.stem: A triploid plant has three homologs for each chromosome. Why does meiosis usually fail to produce balanced gametes?
questions.correct: Homologs cannot pair and segregate evenly, so gametes get variable chromosome numbers.
distractors: Sister chromatids cannot separate because centromeres do not split.
Crossing over cannot occur without exactly two homologs.
Fertilization cannot occur because the plant's gametes are diploid.
questions.why: Meiosis requires homologs to pair and separate; an odd number leaves unpaired chromosomes and uneven segregation. Blaming DNA replication rather than homolog pairing is a common substitution.
options: Sister chromatids cannot separate because centromeres do not split.
Crossing over cannot occur without exactly two homologs.
Homologs cannot pair and segregate evenly, so gametes get variable chromosome numbers.
Fertilization cannot occur because the plant's gametes are diploid.

questions.stem: In a mutant cell with 2n = 8, meiosis I chromosome segregation is normal, but cytokinesis after meiosis I fails. What is the immediate result?
questions.correct: One cell containing two haploid nuclei, each with 4 chromosomes.
distractors: One diploid nucleus with 8 chromosomes.
Two haploid cells, each with 4 chromosomes.
Four haploid nuclei, each with 2 chromosomes.
questions.why: Chromosomes segregate into two haploid nuclei, but the cell does not divide, so both nuclei remain in one cell. The two-cell result describes normal cytokinesis.
options: Four haploid nuclei, each with 2 chromosomes.
One diploid nucleus with 8 chromosomes.
Two haploid cells, each with 4 chromosomes.
One cell containing two haploid nuclei, each with 4 chromosomes.

questions.stem: A human spermatogonium undergoes one mitotic division, and both daughter cells immediately complete meiosis. How many sperm are produced?
questions.correct: 8 sperm
distractors: 4 sperm
2 sperm
16 sperm
questions.why: One spermatogonium gives two primary spermatocytes, and each primary spermatocyte yields four sperm. Forgetting the mitotic division gives 4; doubling twice gives 16.
options: 8 sperm
2 sperm
4 sperm
16 sperm

questions.stem: A mutant prevents cleavage of cohesin along chromosome arms in meiosis I but leaves centromeric cohesin protected normally. What is the most likely result?
questions.correct: Homologs remain joined and fail to separate in anaphase I.
distractors: Sister chromatids separate prematurely in anaphase I.
Crossing over occurs twice as often.
Meiosis II is skipped entirely.
questions.why: Arm cohesin holds homologs together until anaphase I; without its cleavage, homologs cannot separate. The premature-sister result confuses arm cohesin with centromeric cohesin.
options: Sister chromatids separate prematurely in anaphase I.
Homologs remain joined and fail to separate in anaphase I.
Meiosis II is skipped entirely.
Crossing over occurs twice as often.

questions.stem: A human zygote has 47 chromosomes, including three X chromosomes and no Y. The sperm that fertilized it carried one X. What chromosome content did the egg have?
questions.correct: 23 chromosomes, including two X chromosomes.
distractors: 23 chromosomes, including one X chromosome.
24 chromosomes, including one X chromosome.
23 chromosomes, including no X chromosome.
questions.why: The zygote's extra X must have come from the egg, so the egg carried 22 autosomes plus two X chromosomes. An egg with one X would produce a 46,XX zygote.
options: 23 chromosomes, including no X chromosome.
24 chromosomes, including one X chromosome.
23 chromosomes, including two X chromosomes.
23 chromosomes, including one X chromosome.

questions.stem: A human egg with 24 chromosomes is fertilized by a sperm with 22 chromosomes. The zygote has 46 chromosomes. Why is it still considered aneuploid?
questions.correct: It has an extra copy of one chromosome and is missing another, so the set is unbalanced.
distractors: It has 46 chromosomes, so it is a normal diploid.
It is triploid because three chromosome sets are present.
It is haploid because both gametes were abnormal.
questions.why: Aneuploidy is an abnormal chromosome set, not just an abnormal total; the extra and missing chromosomes unbalance the zygote. Counting total chromosomes only would call it normal diploid.
options: It is triploid because three chromosome sets are present.
It has 46 chromosomes, so it is a normal diploid.
It is haploid because both gametes were abnormal.
It has an extra copy of one chromosome and is missing another, so the set is unbalanced.

questions.stem: A drug prevents spindle formation during meiosis II of a fertilized human secondary oocyte. What is the most direct consequence?
questions.correct: Sister chromatids cannot separate, so a haploid ovum and second polar body cannot form.
distractors: Homologs fail to separate, so the oocyte remains diploid.
Crossing over occurs twice as often in prophase II.
The zygote immediately becomes triploid.
questions.why: Meiosis II uses a spindle to separate sister chromatids; without it, the ovum and polar body are not produced. The homolog-separation result confuses meiosis II with meiosis I.
options: Sister chromatids cannot separate, so a haploid ovum and second polar body cannot form.
The zygote immediately becomes triploid.
Homologs fail to separate, so the oocyte remains diploid.
Crossing over occurs twice as often in prophase II.
